salary.page_desc: Calculates your monthly and annual take-home pay after Korea's four social insurance premiums, income tax, and local income tax.
salary.block1_p1: Take-home pay is what actually lands in your bank account after Korea's four social insurance premiums (national pension, health insurance, long-term care insurance, employment insurance), income tax, and local income tax are deducted from your gross (pre-tax) salary. Even at the same gross salary, take-home pay differs based on your number of dependents and social insurance enrollment.
salary.block1_p2: The amount your employer withholds from your pay each month and pays to the government on your behalf is called withholding tax. It's reconciled against your actual tax liability the following year through the year-end tax settlement (연말정산), which either refunds the difference or bills you for it.
salary.block2_p1: Social insurance premiums and income tax are calculated not on your monthly salary (annual salary ÷ 12) but on 'taxable pay' — your monthly salary minus the non-taxable meal allowance (up to 200,000 KRW/month). The meal allowance is money you actually receive, but it's excluded when calculating social insurance premiums and income tax, so leaving it out would understate your true take-home pay.
salary.formula_ltc: Long-Term Care Insurance = Health insurance premium × 13.14%
salary.block2_p2: Income tax is an approximation: the tax base (annual salary minus non-taxable meal allowance, then minus the earned income deduction, personal deductions, etc.) is taxed at the progressive income tax rate (6–45%), then reduced by the earned income tax credit and divided by 12. Local income tax is 10% of the income tax.
salary.block4_title: Income Tax Brackets (2026 Comprehensive Income Tax Rates)
salary.formula_tax: Calculated tax = Tax base × Rate − Progressive deduction
salary.block4_note: These brackets apply to the 'tax base' — your salary minus the earned income deduction, personal deductions, and other deductions — not to your gross annual salary.
salary.faq_q1: Does this result exactly match my actual pay stub?
salary.faq_a1: No — this is an approximation based on the National Tax Service's official rates and deduction rules. Actual withholding follows the simplified withholding tax table the National Tax Service publishes, and depends on whether your employer chose the 80/100/120% withholding option, any non-taxable allowances beyond the meal allowance (e.g. vehicle maintenance, childcare allowances), credit card spending, and other personal deduction items.
salary.faq_q2: Why do I enter a non-taxable meal allowance?
salary.faq_a2: If you don't receive meals directly from your employer, up to 200,000 KRW/month of your meal allowance is excluded not just from income tax but also from the base used to calculate social insurance premiums. Leaving this out understates your take-home pay, so this calculator defaults to 200,000 KRW/month (the non-taxable cap since 2023) and only treats amounts up to that as non-taxable. If your actual meal allowance is different, adjust the field to match.
salary.faq_q3: Why do I enter my number of dependents?
salary.faq_a3: Each dependent gives you a personal deduction of 1,500,000 KRW per year, which lowers your tax base and reduces your income tax. You count as your own dependent, so enter at least 1 even if you have no other dependents.
salary.faq_q4: Why is there a cap on the national pension premium?
salary.faq_a4: National pension premiums aren't based on your actual monthly pay — they're capped within a 'standard monthly income' range, with an upper limit (6,590,000 KRW as of 2026) and a lower limit (410,000 KRW). No matter how high your salary is, your national pension premium won't exceed the amount set by that upper limit.
salary.faq_q5: Should I include bonuses or incentives in my gross annual salary?
salary.faq_a5: Yes. This calculator works from your total annual gross pay, so entering your base salary plus any regular bonuses or performance incentives gives a result closer to your actual average monthly take-home pay.
salary.faq_q6: Does the "Income Tax (XX% bracket)" in the result mean that rate applies to my whole income?
salary.faq_a6: No. Income tax is progressive — each portion of your tax base is taxed at its own bracket's rate. The "XX% bracket" shown is just the highest bracket your tax base reaches (your marginal rate), not a rate applied to your entire income. Lower portions are always taxed at lower rates first, so your effective average rate is always lower than the bracket rate shown.
